title.en: Stress patterns: why рука́ becomes ру́ки

card: Russian stress can move between a word's forms, in a few regular patterns. Nouns: fixed on the stem (**ма́ма, ма́мы**), fixed on the ending (**стол, стола́**), or moving between singular and plural (**окно́ → о́кна**, **рука́ → ру́ки**). Verbs: the **я** form against the rest (**пишу́, пи́шешь**), and the feminine past (**была́**, but **бы́ло**).

sections.body: Stress decides how the vowels sound (an unstressed **о** sounds like **а**) and tells words apart (**за́мок, замо́к**). Native speakers forgive a wrong ending more easily than a wrong stress.

sections.title: Verbs
sections.body: Many verbs stress the ending in the **я** form and the stem in the rest: **пишу́, пи́шешь, пи́шет**; **люблю́, лю́бишь**; **могу́, мо́жешь**. In the past, a group of short verbs stresses the feminine ending: **был, была́, бы́ло, бы́ли**; **взял, взяла́**; **жил, жила́**; **на́чал, начала́**.

sections.title: Short adjectives
sections.body: Short adjectives often stress the feminine ending: **мо́лод, молода́, мо́лодо, мо́лоды**; **прав, права́**.

Learn three forms of each new noun: the nominative singular, the genitive singular and the nominative plural (**рука́, руки́, ру́ки**). For verbs, learn the infinitive and the **я** and **ты** forms (**писа́ть, пишу́, пи́шешь**). Together they show the pattern.
